interactions.summary: The reading finishes Statius and Virgil’s exchange, turns toward the terrace of gluttony, and lists scriptural examples of disciplined abstinence before John the Baptist.
Jiang pauses the gluttony scene to reopen the larger heaven paradox, jumping to Paradise 20 and the eagle of righteous rulers as evidence that secret conversion is not the whole solution.

speaker_notes.note: The reading is noisy and overlong in the list of poets, but the scene-level movement is clear: poetic conversation ends when the travelers reach the gluttony tree.

claims.claim: The gluttony terrace is staged around a fruit tree that intensifies desire precisely by denying satisfaction.
Jiang says Statius’s secret conversion only seems to solve the access-to-heaven paradox, because Paradise still contains figures whose cases are harder to explain.
Jiang points to the eagle in Paradise 20 as a text Dante uses to force the question of how non-Christians or pre-Christians can still appear among the blessed.

signature_moments.moment: The tree of gluttony trains hunger by dangling fruit that must never be touched.
signature_moments.source_phrase: there's a tree with lots of fruit and the sinners just look at it
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This compresses Jiang’s reading of purgatorial pedagogy: desire is intensified in order to be reordered.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang widens the puzzle from one secret Christian to the whole eagle of history.
signature_moments.source_phrase: this is really confusing now for us
signature_moments.why_it_matters: He deliberately uses Dante’s paradise as a pressure test against narrow gatekeeping theology.

chronology_notes.note: This packet marks Jiang’s transition from the Statius case to a broader June 26 doctrine of salvation that will not stay contained within formal Christian identity.

uncertainty_notes.note: The roster of classical names is ASR-noisy, but it does not affect the main semantic movement into the gluttony scene.
